# Payments Architecture

This document captures the high-level design of the payments subsystem.

It is the canonical reference for engineers building or changing payment flows.

## Overview

The payments stack is split into three layers: the public API, the orchestration
core, and the downstream provider adapters. Each layer has its own deployment
unit and its own ownership boundary. The boundaries are policy boundaries, not
just packaging boundaries — a change in one layer must not silently impose new
expectations on another. Cross-layer concerns are negotiated explicitly through
the contracts in this document.

## Authentication

All inbound payment requests are authenticated against the central identity
service before any business logic runs. The identity service issues short-lived
bearer tokens scoped to specific tenants and signed with rotating keys. Tokens
are validated at the API gateway and propagated to downstream services as
opaque context headers; downstream code never re-validates the bearer itself.
Token expiry is enforced at the gateway with a five-second clock-skew window.

## Payment Processing

The payment-processing path is the load-bearing flow for the whole subsystem.
Inbound transactions are accepted by the API layer, normalised into the
internal `PaymentIntent` shape, and handed to `src/payments/processor.ts` for
dispatch.

Historically `src/payments/processor.ts` exposed a single batched entry point
named `processPaymentBatch` that grouped multiple intents and submitted them
as one call to the provider. The batched path was retired during the 2025-Q4
reliability work — provider-side rate limits made per-transaction dispatch
more predictable than batch-of-N, and per-transaction telemetry is now
strictly required by the compliance team.

The current entry point is `processPaymentTransactions`. It accepts the same
`PaymentIntent[]` shape as the old batch call but iterates internally,
dispatching one transaction at a time and emitting one telemetry record per
transaction. Callers that previously called `processPaymentBatch` MUST be
migrated; there is no shim and no dual-write fallback.

## Notifications

The notifications layer fans out asynchronously from completed payment events.
A dedicated worker subscribes to the `payments.completed` topic and writes
email and SMS notifications via the messaging provider. Notification failures
are retried with exponential backoff up to six attempts; after the final
failure the event is parked on a dead-letter queue and on-call is paged.

## Reporting

Aggregated reporting runs nightly against the read replica. The reporting
pipeline emits four canonical tables consumed by the finance and product
analytics teams: daily totals, per-tenant volume, dispute counts, and
provider-side latency percentiles. Reporting never reads the primary; the
reporting account has read-replica-only credentials by policy.

## Compliance

Compliance evidence is generated on every payment-state transition. The
compliance log is append-only, stored on the immutable bucket, and exported
to the auditor's pipeline once per quarter. The auditor's pipeline is the
authoritative source for SOC 2 evidence — internal queries against the
compliance log are advisory only.

## Glossary

Tenant — workspace boundary; the multi-tenancy unit.
Workspace — primary container for users, projects, and settings.
Quota — per-tenant resource ceiling enforced by the gateway.
Webhook — outbound HTTP callback delivered to a tenant endpoint.
Audit — append-only event stream consumed by the compliance pipeline.

# Billing FAQ

This document answers frequently asked questions about the customer billing
experience. It is owned by the support enablement team and is reviewed
quarterly.

## How do customers update their card?

Customers update their payment method from the account settings page under the
"Billing" tab. Updating the card triggers a zero-amount authorisation against
the new card to validate that it is live; the authorisation is reversed
immediately. The card-on-file is rotated atomically — there is no period
during which both the old and the new card are simultaneously active.

The update flow is fully self-serve. Support agents do not have the ability
to enter card details on behalf of a customer; this is deliberate and is
audited regularly. If a customer cannot complete the update themselves they
must be directed to the assisted-update form, which generates a one-time
secure link they can use without an account login.

Updates that fail the validation authorisation surface the provider's failure
reason verbatim. The most common reasons are insufficient funds (transient,
retry tomorrow), incorrect billing address (correct and re-submit), and
expired card (use a non-expired card). Provider-issued failure reasons are
not localised by the billing service — they appear in English regardless of
the customer's preferred language.

## What happens when a card expires?

The billing service watches the upcoming-expiry signal and sends a reminder
email forty-five days, fifteen days, and three days before the expiry date.
If the card has not been updated by the expiry date, the next renewal attempt
is dunned: the system retries once a day for seven days, escalates to a
support ticket on day eight, and downgrades the workspace to read-only on
day fifteen.

The forty-five-day reminder is intentionally aggressive. Customer surveys
showed that a single seven-day reminder produced too many last-minute support
tickets. The cadence is reviewed annually with the support enablement team
and may be tuned per region in future versions of the billing service.

Downgrade to read-only is reversible. A successful renewal payment within
sixty days of the downgrade restores full workspace access without data loss.
After sixty days the workspace enters a deletion queue and is purged after
an additional thirty days; that purge is irreversible.

## Can customers see their invoice history?

Customer invoice history is available under the "Billing" tab in account
settings. The interface lists the most recent thirty-six invoices by default;
older invoices are available on request through the support team. Each invoice
links to a downloadable PDF and to a CSV breakdown of line items.

Invoice numbering is sequential per workspace and never reused. A cancelled
invoice retains its number and is marked "VOID" with the cancellation reason
and the cancelling agent recorded on the invoice itself. The CSV breakdown
mirrors the PDF totals exactly; any discrepancy between the two is a billing
service bug and should be reported to support.

## How are taxes applied?

Tax computation is delegated to the tax provider on a per-invoice basis. The
provider determines the applicable jurisdictions from the customer's billing
address and applies the relevant rates. The displayed total on the invoice is
authoritative — internal subtotals are advisory.

Tax-exempt workspaces upload their certificate to the tax provider's portal
and the certificate is associated with the workspace's tax-provider record.
Once associated, future invoices for that workspace are issued without tax
lines. Certificate expiry is tracked by the tax provider; the billing service
trusts the provider's status signal on every invoice.

## What if a customer disputes a charge?

Disputes are recorded in the disputes module under "Billing then Disputes."
The support team triages the dispute, gathers evidence (usage logs, contract
PDFs, email correspondence), and responds through the provider's dispute
interface. The provider's final decision is recorded against the dispute and
the customer is notified by email.

Disputes have a strict response window that varies by card network. The
disputes dashboard surfaces the per-dispute deadline prominently and pages
the on-call support engineer four hours before the deadline if no response
has been filed. Missing the deadline forfeits the dispute by default.

## Are refunds supported?

Refunds are supported in full or in part. Partial refunds require a written
justification recorded against the refund record for audit purposes. Refunds
are issued to the original payment method; refunds to a different method
require manager approval and a documented reason.

Refund timing depends on the provider and the card-issuer combination.
Customers typically see the refund within five business days; some
international issuers take up to fifteen business days. The billing service
does not retry a refund — once issued, the refund record is terminal and any
follow-up is handled manually by the finance team.

## How are trial periods billed?

Trial periods are tracked as a separate trial state on the workspace record.
No card is charged during the trial. On trial completion, the workspace
transitions to the paid plan, the card-on-file is charged for the first
billing period, and the standard renewal cadence takes over from there.

Customers can extend a trial once, by up to fourteen days, through the
self-serve trial dashboard. Beyond fourteen days, an extension requires a
support ticket and a documented sales rationale. Extensions are recorded
against the workspace's trial history so future quarters' analytics can
attribute them correctly.

## How is annual prepayment handled?

Annual prepayment is a single charge at the start of the contract year. The
invoice is dated on the contract start date and the line items reflect the
annual commitment. Mid-year plan changes are pro-rated against the remaining
balance on the prepayment and either credited or charged on the next monthly
invoice.

Annual prepayment customers receive a discount applied as a percentage of
the annual rate, recorded on the invoice as a single "annual commitment
credit" line. The discount percentage is set by the sales contract and is
not editable by the billing service — sales must amend the contract to
change the discount.

## What about non-card payment methods?

Bank transfer and direct debit are supported for annual contracts above the
self-serve threshold. Customers on these methods receive an invoice with
payment instructions; the workspace is not provisioned until payment is
received and reconciled by the finance team. Self-serve customers must use
a card.

The reconciliation cadence for bank transfer is one business day. Customers
who pay by transfer should expect their workspace to be provisioned the
business day after the funds arrive in the finance team's account.
Pre-payment is permitted; the funds sit as a credit on the workspace until
the next invoice cycle consumes them.

## How do I cancel a subscription?

Cancellation is self-serve from the "Billing" tab. The cancellation form
asks for a reason from a fixed list and an optional free-text comment.
The cancellation is effective at the end of the current billing period;
no pro-rated refund is issued for the unused portion of the period.

Cancellations can be reversed within the first seven days through a support
ticket. After seven days the workspace enters the deletion queue and the
cancellation is final. Customers who change their mind after the deletion
queue starts must open a new workspace and re-provision from scratch.

## What about purchase orders?

Purchase orders are accepted for annual contracts only. The customer's
procurement team submits the PO to the finance mailbox, the finance team
validates the PO against the signed contract, and the workspace is
provisioned once both signatures are in place. PO numbers are recorded
on every invoice issued against the contract.

The minimum contract value for PO billing is set by sales policy and is
reviewed annually. Below the minimum, customers must use a card or a
bank-transfer arrangement; the finance team does not maintain PO records
below the minimum value.

## How do credits work?

Workspace credits are applied automatically against the next invoice.
Credits are typically issued for service-level breaches, customer-success
gestures, or unused prepayment balances on plan downgrades. The credit
amount and the issuing reason are recorded on the credit record and
displayed on the next invoice as a single line.

Credits expire twelve months after issuance. Expired credits are not
refundable; they simply lapse from the workspace's credit balance. The
billing service emails the workspace billing contact thirty days before
any credit is set to expire.

## What does the "billing contact" do?

The billing contact is the named individual on the workspace's billing
record who receives all billing emails: invoices, expiry reminders, dunning
notices, dispute updates, credit issuance, and credit expiry. The billing
contact does not need to be the workspace owner; many workspaces designate
a finance team member.

The billing contact is editable from the "Billing" tab by anyone with the
"manage-billing" permission. Changing the contact does not retroactively
re-send historical emails; the new contact begins receiving notifications
from the next event onwards.

# Deployment Runbook

This runbook is the canonical checklist for production deployments. It is
owned by the platform team and reviewed monthly with the on-call rotation.

## Preconditions

Before kicking off a production deployment the engineer-on-call confirms the
release window is open, the staging environment has been green for at least
two hours, and there are no active incidents above severity three. The change
ticket must be approved by both the engineering reviewer and the change
manager. A merge to main without the change ticket is a process violation.

The release window is defined in the calendar maintained by the platform
team. Out-of-window deployments are reserved for hotfixes and security
patches and require an additional approver from the security team. The
calendar is maintained six weeks ahead so engineering teams can plan
their release cadence around it.

Staging-green is determined by the staging dashboard and includes the full
post-merge smoke suite plus the canary observability checks. A flake on a
known-unstable smoke test is acceptable only if the test owner has filed a
quarantine ticket and the quarantine has been approved by the platform
team. Unsanctioned flakes block deployment.

## Build verification

The build pipeline produces a container image, a static-asset bundle, and a
migration plan. All three artefacts are tagged with the same release tag. The
engineer-on-call verifies the image SHA matches the digest recorded in the
release ticket and that the migration plan does not include any unreviewed
schema changes. A migration plan with even a single unreviewed change blocks
the deployment until the change is reviewed.

Image provenance is enforced by the registry's signature requirement. Only
images signed by the build pipeline's key are accepted by the production
runtime. Engineers cannot push images directly to the production registry;
the only path is through the pipeline. This is an audited control.

## Rollout strategy

Rollout follows a canary-then-bulk pattern. The canary instance receives one
percent of traffic for fifteen minutes; the engineer-on-call watches the
golden-signal dashboard. If error rate, p99 latency, or saturation exceeds
the canary thresholds the rollout is aborted and rolled back automatically.
On a clean canary the bulk rollout proceeds in waves of twenty percent until
the new version is at one hundred percent of traffic.

Wave timing is paced to allow each wave's observability signals to stabilise
before the next wave begins. The default pacing is five minutes between
waves; release tags marked as high-risk by the engineering reviewer use a
ten-minute pacing instead. The pacing is recorded in the release ticket so
post-deployment review can audit it.

The canary instance is selected at random from the fleet's least-recently-
deployed pool. This avoids a deterministic canary instance becoming an
ad-hoc "test instance" with stale state. Random selection is logged in
the deployment record for traceability.

## Database migrations

Database migrations are applied before the application rollout begins. The
migrations module enforces backwards-compatible changes only — any backwards-
incompatible migration must be split into a compatible expand stage, a code
rollout, and a contract stage in a later release. The expand-contract pattern
is non-negotiable for production schemas.

The migration runner is idempotent. Re-running the same migration plan
against the same schema state is a no-op. The runner records every executed
migration's name and timestamp in the `schema_migrations` table; the table
is queried by the runner before each batch to skip already-applied
migrations.

Migration failure aborts the deployment. The runner logs the failing
migration and the offending error, leaves the schema in its last-known-good
state (transactional migrations) or in an explicitly-marked partial state
(non-transactional migrations), and pages the database on-call. The
deployment cannot proceed until the migration is either fixed or rolled back.

## Feature flags

Feature flags ship in the off state by default. The engineer-on-call records
which flags are being turned on during the deployment and the rollout cadence
for each flag. Flag rollouts are independent of the deployment itself — a
flag can be flipped without a code deploy if the flag is already shipped.

Flag rollouts above five percent of traffic require an additional reviewer
sign-off. The reviewer reviews the flag's observability dashboard and signs
off in the flag-management tool. Flags above twenty-five percent require
sign-off from the platform team in addition.

Stale flags are audited quarterly. A flag that has been at one-hundred
percent for more than three quarters is a candidate for retirement; the
engineering team owning the flag must either retire it or document why it
should remain. Indefinite live flags are a tech-debt liability and the
audit exists specifically to surface them.

## Monitoring

During and after a deployment the engineer-on-call watches three dashboards:
the golden-signal dashboard (error rate, latency, saturation), the per-tenant
volume dashboard, and the integrations dashboard. Any anomaly above the
documented thresholds triggers the rollback runbook. Anomalies below the
thresholds are noted in the deployment log for follow-up.

The golden-signal dashboard panels are configured with deployment-aware
annotations. Each annotation marks the start and end of a wave so the
engineer-on-call can correlate signal changes with the rollout phase. The
annotations are emitted automatically by the deployment pipeline; no manual
intervention is required.

The integrations dashboard surfaces every external dependency's health
indicator alongside the deployment's own signals. A dependency degradation
during a deployment is treated as a separate incident — the engineer-on-call
does not roll back unless the deployment itself is implicated.

## Rollback

Rollback is triggered automatically by the canary guardrails. Manual rollback
is also available through the deployment dashboard. A manual rollback
requires confirmation from a second engineer. Rollbacks reverse the
application deploy first; database rollbacks are a separate, escalated
procedure that requires the database on-call to attend.

The rollback target is the previous green release tag. Rolling back further
than one release requires explicit approval from the engineering reviewer
and a re-validation of the staging environment against the older tag. This
multi-step rollback is rare and is reserved for genuinely unrecoverable
regressions.

Post-rollback the deployment record is annotated with the rollback reason,
the rolling engineer, and the time-to-detect and time-to-rollback measurements.
These measurements feed the monthly reliability review and the operational
metrics dashboard.

## Post-deployment review

After every production deployment the engineer-on-call writes a short post-
deployment note in the deployment log. The note records the start and end
time, any anomalies observed, any guardrails that fired, and any follow-up
work generated. The notes feed into the monthly reliability review.

Notes that record an automatic rollback or a manual rollback always trigger
a post-incident review the following business day. The review is led by the
engineering reviewer and includes the engineer-on-call, the deploying team,
and a member of the platform team. The review's output is a written incident
report archived alongside the deployment log.

## Out-of-hours deployments

Out-of-hours deployments are reserved for security patches and severity-one
hotfixes. Any other change waits for the next in-hours window. The on-call
rotation is staffed during business hours; the out-of-hours rotation is
strictly for incidents.

Security patches that must be deployed out-of-hours are coordinated through
the security team's on-call channel. The security team supplies the
justification, the engineering team supplies the patch, and the deploying
engineer follows the same canary-then-bulk pattern as in-hours deployments.
There is no shortcut to canary even for security work.

## Communication

Deployments are announced in the deployments channel ten minutes before the
canary begins. The announcement names the release tag, the engineer-on-call,
and the change ticket. A second announcement names the rollout end and any
notable observations. Silent deployments are forbidden.

The deployments channel is read-only for non-engineering teams. Read access
is broad — product, support, and customer-success all subscribe — but write
access is gated to engineers and the platform team. This keeps the channel
high-signal during incidents.

A weekly digest of deployments is posted to the internal-news channel every
Friday. The digest names every deployment of the week, the team that owned
it, and any notable post-deployment observations. The digest is generated
automatically from the deployment log; no manual curation is required.

## Hotfix workflow

Hotfixes follow an accelerated workflow. The change ticket is opened in the
hotfix queue, the engineering reviewer signs off, and the deployment runs
within thirty minutes of sign-off. The canary still applies — there is no
"skip canary" option for hotfixes — but the wave pacing is collapsed to two
minutes between waves to expedite the rollout.

Hotfix deployments are audited weekly. A surge in hotfix frequency is a
process smell; the platform team raises it with the relevant engineering
manager as a leading indicator of an underlying reliability issue.

## Multi-region considerations

Multi-region deployments roll out region by region rather than globally
in one wave. The first region is selected as the smallest by traffic so a
regression is contained. After the first region holds for fifteen minutes
without anomalies the second region begins, and so on through the rotation.

Regional rollout pacing can be paused between regions. A pause is requested
through the deployment dashboard; the pause requires no second sign-off and
can be lifted at any time by the deploying engineer. Paused deployments
older than four hours expire and revert to the last-deployed region.
